seatMission: Prioritize the next vital need and reduce owner dependence.
seatResponsibilities: Identify next vital need, profit discipline, scaling rhythm and owner independence.

criterionDimensions.name: Next vital need and constraint diagnosis

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I identify the business's current limiting need before prescribing growth initiatives that may optimize the wrong layer.
I distinguish survival, stability, profitability, order, impact, and legacy problems instead of treating every constraint as a sales problem.
I use evidence from cash, demand, delivery, quality, people, and owner workload to locate the next vital constraint.
I test whether the apparent bottleneck is causal, consequential, and currently binding rather than merely visible.
I rank competing needs by their effect on business survival, throughput, profitability, and owner dependence.
I avoid solving higher-order growth problems while foundational cash, fulfillment, or control failures remain unresolved.
I define the observable condition that would show the current vital need has been sufficiently addressed.
I revisit the constraint after material changes because the next limiting need can move as the business improves.
I separate chronic structural constraints from temporary incidents that require containment but not redesign.
I convert constraint diagnosis into a bounded sequence of priorities rather than a simultaneous transformation wish list.
I treat profitability as an operating discipline rather than a year-end accounting surprise.
I distinguish revenue growth from profitable growth and require contribution evidence before celebrating scale.
I identify customers, offers, channels, activities, and overhead that consume more value than they create.
I make margin leakage visible through discounting, rework, refunds, service burden, waste, and unmanaged complexity.
I define profit targets and allocation rules that influence day-to-day operating choices without hiding obligations or starving critical capability.
I use unit economics and cash timing to test whether growth strengthens or weakens the company.
I separate necessary investment from habitual spending and require a decision rationale for material recurring cost.
I protect the business from using future hoped-for revenue to justify structurally unaffordable present commitments.
I monitor profitability by meaningful segment or activity when blended averages conceal destructive cross-subsidies.
I redesign the operating model when profit depends primarily on heroic effort, unpaid owner labor, or unsustainable exceptions.
I test whether planned growth can be funded from available cash, contribution, financing capacity, and working capital without threatening survival.
I sequence investments so scarce cash goes first to the constraint whose removal creates the greatest durable capacity or value.
I distinguish growth capital from cash required to repair operational debt, compliance gaps, or past underinvestment.
I model the cash lag between acquisition spending, delivery, invoicing, collection, refunds, and retained contribution.
I define funding thresholds and stop conditions before accelerating demand or headcount.
I preserve liquidity buffers proportionate to volatility, concentration, fixed obligations, and recovery options.
I compare internal funding, debt, equity, vendor terms, customer financing, and staged investment by cost, control, risk, and flexibility.
I avoid funding growth with obligations whose downside exceeds the business's credible repayment capacity.
I prioritize experiments and reversible investments when the economics of scale are not yet demonstrated.
I require evidence that incremental capital actually improves the limiting constraint rather than adding parallel activity around it.
I identify functions, decisions, relationships, and knowledge that depend materially on the owner and therefore constrain transferability.
I distinguish legitimate owner governance from avoidable owner involvement in routine execution.
I convert owner-only knowledge into explicit policies, decision criteria, playbooks, data, or delegated authority where appropriate.
I assign accountable owners for recurring outcomes instead of routing every exception to the founder.
I define decision boundaries that allow delegation without requiring constant permission or creating uncontrolled autonomy.
I test delegated processes under realistic conditions before declaring the business independent of the owner.
I build management capability so the owner can exit operational loops without causing hidden quality or customer failures.
I measure owner dependence through observable intervention frequency, decision latency, escalations, and unavailable-time failure.
I remove incentives that reward employees for escalating solvable work upward instead of owning bounded decisions.
I preserve the owner's unique strategic contributions while eliminating owner presence as a prerequisite for normal delivery.
I standardize recurring work when variation does not create customer or strategic value.
I distinguish standard work from rigid bureaucracy and retain explicit exception paths for cases that genuinely differ.
I design operating cadences that convert priorities into recurring commitments, review, learning, and correction.
I reduce dependence on memory by making critical workflows, controls, definitions, and handoffs explicit.
I automate only after understanding the real process, decision points, exceptions, and failure recovery.
I use simple visible operating rhythms before adding complex coordination mechanisms that create more overhead than control.
I measure cycle time, quality, backlog, exceptions, and rework to determine whether standardization improves actual delivery.
I align meeting cadence with decision frequency and remove meetings that produce neither decisions nor accountable follow-through.
I version operating procedures when evidence changes the best-known method rather than preserving obsolete consistency.
I design routines that remain usable during peak load, absence, turnover, and difficult operating days.
I identify customers whose revenue is outweighed by discounting, service burden, payment risk, churn, reputational risk, or strategic distraction.
I distinguish a difficult but valuable customer from a structurally unprofitable or misaligned customer.
I identify products, services, channels, projects, and internal activities that consume scarce capacity without sufficient value.
I evaluate the opportunity cost of keeping low-value work before adding more people to accommodate it.
I stop or simplify offerings whose complexity exceeds their economic or strategic contribution.
I preserve evidence about why an activity was removed so it is not reintroduced later without new justification.
I use concentration and dependency analysis before pruning revenue sources that may create unacceptable transition risk.
I improve pricing, scope, service levels, or operating rules before abandoning customers when the economics can be repaired.
I reject vanity growth that expands volume while worsening margin, cash, quality, or owner dependence.
I define explicit keep, fix, harvest, partner, or exit decisions for materially underperforming activities.
I distinguish theoretical capacity from dependable capacity after downtime, variation, training, quality, and exception handling.
I identify the true system bottleneck and avoid optimizing non-bottleneck resources merely to increase local utilization.
I test whether demand growth will move the bottleneck into fulfillment, support, working capital, management, or another downstream function.
I model step costs and capacity thresholds so scale plans do not assume smooth linear economics.
I measure queue growth, cycle time, rework, and service degradation as early signals that scale is outrunning capacity.
I prefer debottlenecking, simplification, scheduling, and process redesign before defaulting to headcount expansion.
I evaluate whether automation increases total system throughput or merely makes one local activity faster.
I incorporate supplier, partner, technology, and regulatory capacity constraints into scale planning.
I preserve slack where it improves resilience, responsiveness, learning, or quality rather than maximizing utilization everywhere.
I validate economies of scale with actual cost and performance evidence instead of assuming larger volume automatically improves margins.
I translate strategic priorities into a small number of accountable operating commitments with named owners and measurable outcomes.
I distinguish leading indicators, lagging results, and guardrails so teams know what can be influenced now and what confirms later success.
I define metrics with stable semantics, data sources, cadence, thresholds, and decision actions.
I use recurring reviews to resolve constraints and commitments rather than to narrate status already available elsewhere.
I expose missed commitments without converting accountability into blame or hiding systemic causes.
I maintain a visible record of decisions, owners, due dates, dependencies, and unresolved blockers.
I escalate only when authority, dependency, risk, or repeated failure exceeds the team's bounded ability to resolve the issue.
I reduce management overhead when a governance mechanism no longer improves coordination, control, or learning.
I align incentives with profitable, durable outcomes rather than isolated volume, utilization, or activity metrics.
I require management systems to remain understandable and executable without the founder personally interpreting every dashboard.
I define where the business will focus and what it will deliberately stop pursuing so scale reinforces rather than dilutes advantage.
I identify a repeatable customer, offer, channel, and delivery pattern before assuming growth can be replicated.
I distinguish one-time wins from a repeatable growth engine supported by consistent economics and operating capability.
I protect strategic capacity from excessive customization that turns every sale into a new business model.
I standardize the repeatable core while allowing bounded adaptation for segments or contexts that genuinely require it.
I test whether increased volume strengthens purchasing power, learning, network effects, brand, data, or another defensible advantage.
I avoid expansion into new markets, products, or channels when the existing engine is not yet operationally stable.
I sequence growth initiatives according to constraint removal and capability readiness rather than executive enthusiasm.
I use experiments to prove expansion assumptions before committing irreversible scale.
I monitor whether scale is increasing customer value and strategic strength, not merely organizational size.
I design the company so critical outcomes can continue through owner absence, leadership turnover, supplier failure, demand shocks, and other foreseeable disruptions.
I reduce single-person dependencies in knowledge, authority, customer relationships, credentials, and operational access.
I establish succession and backup arrangements proportionate to the consequences of losing a key role.
I distinguish scalable independence from disengagement and preserve clear governance, accountability, and strategic direction.
I maintain enough documented institutional memory that a competent successor can reconstruct important decisions and operating logic.
I test continuity under absence or failure instead of assuming documented procedures prove resilience.
I develop leaders who can diagnose constraints and adapt systems rather than merely follow the founder's historical instructions.
I protect transferability by reducing undocumented exceptions, informal side agreements, and owner-specific customer promises.
I measure progress toward independence through reduced intervention, faster local decisions, stable quality, and preserved economics.
I treat legacy readiness as the ability to create value beyond the current owner, not merely the owner's intention to sell or retire.
